title: Web and backend
summary: HTTP, JSON, URLs, WSGI, Flask and how Django routes requests.

lessons.title: HTTP and JSON
lessons.body:
# HTTP and JSON

HTTP is text exchanged in pairs. A request has a method, a path, headers and an optional body. A response has a status code, headers and a body.

- `GET` reads, `POST` creates, `PUT` replaces, `DELETE` removes.
- `2xx` means success, `4xx` a client mistake, and `5xx` a server failure.
- `Content-Type` says how to interpret the body.

Most APIs send JSON. The `json` module converts between JSON text and Python values.

```python
import json

text = json.dumps({"id": 1, "ok": True})
print(text)  # {"id": 1, "ok": true}
data = json.loads(text)
print(data["ok"])  # True
```

## What changes on the way

- `None` becomes `null`, and tuples become arrays.
- Dict keys become strings, so `{1: "a"}` returns as `{"1": "a"}`.
- Types with no JSON form, such as a `set`, raise `TypeError`.
- Bad input raises `json.JSONDecodeError`, a subclass of `ValueError`.
lessons.task: Write `make_response(data, status=200)` returning a dict with `status`, `headers` (`{"Content-Type": "application/json"}`) and `body` as compact JSON text with sorted keys. Write `read_response(response)` returning the parsed body, raising `ValueError` for status 400 or above (including the body's `error` value if it has one) or for invalid JSON.

checks.name: builds a response
checks.code:
got = make_response({"b": 1, "a": 2})
assert got["status"] == 200, got
assert got["headers"] == {"Content-Type": "application/json"}, got
assert got["body"] == '{"a":2,"b":1}', got["body"]

checks.name: round trip
checks.code: assert read_response(make_response([1, None, "x"])) == [1, None, "x"], "values should survive"

checks.name: dict keys become strings
checks.code: assert read_response(make_response({1: "a"})) == {"1": "a"}, "JSON keys are strings"

checks.name: error statuses raise with the message
checks.code:
message = None
try:
    read_response(make_response({"error": "no such item"}, status=404))
except ValueError as error:
    message = str(error)
assert message is not None, "status 404 should raise ValueError"
assert "no such item" in message, message

checks.name: error status with a non-JSON body
invalid JSON raises ValueError

hints: `JSONDecodeError` is already a `ValueError`, but a server error page may not be JSON at all, so the error path must not depend on parsing.

Parse inside `try`. On failure, set `data = None` and re-raise only if the status is below 400. Then, if the status is 400 or above, raise `ValueError` using `data.get("error", ...)` when `data` is a dict.
lessons.explanation:
Parsing is done before the status test so an error body can supply a helpful message, but a failure to parse must not hide the real error. Proxies and crashed servers often answer with HTML.

Sorted keys and compact separators make the output byte-for-byte predictable, which helps with tests, caching and signatures.

lessons.title: Parsing a URL
lessons.body:
# Parsing a URL

Never take URLs apart with `split`. Encoding rules and optional parts make that fragile. `urllib.parse` handles them.

```python
from urllib.parse import (
    urlsplit, parse_qsl, urlencode)

u = urlsplit(
    "https://a.io:8000/s?q=a+b&p=2#top")
print(u.scheme, u.hostname, u.port)
print(u.path, u.query, u.fragment)
print(parse_qsl(u.query))
# [('q', 'a b'), ('p', '2')]
print(urlencode({"q": "a b"}))
# q=a+b
```

- `u.port` is `None` when the URL does not state one.
- `parse_qsl` drops parameters with blank values unless you pass `keep_blank_values=True`.
- `parse_qs` returns a dict of lists, since a key may repeat.
- A split URL is a named tuple, so `u._replace(query="x=1").geturl()` builds a new URL with one part changed.

`quote` and `unquote` handle percent-encoding, and `urljoin` resolves relative links.
lessons.task: Write `query_params(url)` returning a dict from each key to its first value, keeping blank values. Write `add_param(url, key, value)` setting one query parameter, replacing it in place if present, otherwise appending, and leaving other URL parts alone. Write `host_and_port(url)` returning `(host, port)`, using 443 for https and 80 for http when none is given.

checks.name: decodes values
checks.code:
got = query_params("https://a.io/s?q=caf%C3%A9+au+lait&p=2")
assert got == {"q": "café au lait", "p": "2"}, got

checks.name: edge cases in queries
checks.code:
assert query_params("https://a.io/") == {}, query_params("https://a.io/")
assert query_params("/s?empty=&x=1") == {"empty": "", "x": "1"}, query_params("/s?empty=&x=1")
assert query_params("/s?a=1&a=2") == {"a": "1"}, query_params("/s?a=1&a=2")

checks.name: query_params ignores the fragment
checks.code: assert query_params("/s?a=1#b=2") == {"a": "1"}, query_params("/s?a=1#b=2")

checks.name: add_param appends and encodes
checks.code:
got = add_param("https://a.io/", "q", "a b")
assert got == "https://a.io/?q=a+b", got
got = add_param("https://a.io/s?x=1", "y", "2")
assert got == "https://a.io/s?x=1&y=2", got

checks.name: add_param replaces in place and keeps the fragment
checks.code:
got = add_param("https://a.io/s?q=1&p=2&z=3#top", "p", "9")
assert got == "https://a.io/s?q=1&p=9&z=3#top", got

checks.name: host and port
checks.code:
assert host_and_port("https://example.com/x") == ("example.com", 443), host_and_port("https://example.com/x")
assert host_and_port("http://example.com") == ("example.com", 80), host_and_port("http://example.com")
assert host_and_port("http://localhost:8000/") == ("localhost", 8000), host_and_port("http://localhost:8000/")

hints: `urlsplit(url).query` isolates the query string, whether or not there is a fragment. `parse_qsl` decodes it into pairs.
A dict keeps insertion order, so assigning to an existing key keeps its place. `_replace` on the split result swaps one part.

For `query_params`, loop over the pairs with `result.setdefault(key, value)`. For `add_param`, `params = dict(parse_qsl(parts.query, keep_blank_values=True))`, set the key, then `parts._replace(query=urlencode(params)).geturl()`.
lessons.explanation:
`urlsplit` knows where each part starts, so a `#` in the fragment or a missing `?` needs no special handling. `parse_qsl` undoes `+` and percent-encoding, and `urlencode` applies them again, so values stay correct in both directions.

`setdefault` keeps the first value when a key repeats, whereas `dict(pairs)` would keep the last.

lessons.title: WSGI
lessons.body:
# WSGI

WSGI is the standard interface between Python web apps and servers. An app is one callable with this shape:

```python
def app(environ, start_response):
    start_response(
        "200 OK",
        [("Content-Type", "text/plain")],
    )
    return [b"hello"]
```

- `environ` is a dict describing the request, with keys such as `REQUEST_METHOD`, `PATH_INFO` and `QUERY_STRING`.
- `start_response(status, headers)` sets the status line and a list of header tuples.
- The return value is an iterable of `bytes`.

Flask and Django are both WSGI apps underneath, and a server such as gunicorn just calls this function once per request.

Since it is only a function, you can test it with no server and no network. Build an `environ` dict, pass a `start_response` that records its arguments, and join the returned bytes.
lessons.task: Write a WSGI function `app`. `GET /` returns `200 OK` with body `hello`. `GET /echo?msg=x` returns `200 OK` with the decoded value of `msg` as UTF-8 (empty if absent). Any other path returns `404 Not Found`. A method other than GET returns `405 Method Not Allowed` with an `Allow: GET` header. Every response has `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8`.

checks.name: home page
checks.code:
started = []
body = app({"REQUEST_METHOD": "GET", "PATH_INFO": "/", "QUERY_STRING": ""}, lambda s, h: started.append((s, h)))
assert started[0][0] == "200 OK", started
assert b"".join(body) == b"hello", body

checks.name: content type on every response
checks.code:
for method, path in [("GET", "/"), ("GET", "/nope"), ("POST", "/")]:
    started = []
    app({"REQUEST_METHOD": method, "PATH_INFO": path, "QUERY_STRING": ""}, lambda s, h: started.append((s, h)))
    headers = dict(started[0][1])
    assert headers.get("Content-Type") == "text/plain; charset=utf-8", (method, path, headers)

checks.name: echo decodes the query
checks.code:
started = []
query = "msg=caf%C3%A9+now"
body = app({"REQUEST_METHOD": "GET", "PATH_INFO": "/echo", "QUERY_STRING": query}, lambda s, h: started.append((s, h)))
assert started[0][0] == "200 OK", started
assert b"".join(body) == "café now".encode("utf-8"), body

checks.name: echo with no msg
checks.code:
started = []
body = app({"REQUEST_METHOD": "GET", "PATH_INFO": "/echo"}, lambda s, h: started.append((s, h)))
assert started[0][0] == "200 OK", started
assert b"".join(body) == b"", body

checks.name: unknown path is 404
checks.code:
started = []
app({"REQUEST_METHOD": "GET", "PATH_INFO": "/nope", "QUERY_STRING": ""}, lambda s, h: started.append((s, h)))
assert started[0][0] == "404 Not Found", started

checks.name: wrong method is 405
checks.code:
started = []
app({"REQUEST_METHOD": "POST", "PATH_INFO": "/echo", "QUERY_STRING": ""}, lambda s, h: started.append((s, h)))
assert started[0][0] == "405 Method Not Allowed", started
assert dict(started[0][1]).get("Allow") == "GET", started

hints: Decide the status, headers and text first, then call `start_response` once and return a list holding encoded bytes.
Test the method before the path, since a POST to any path is a 405. `QUERY_STRING` may be missing, so use `environ.get`.
`parse_qs(environ.get("QUERY_STRING", ""))` returns a dict of lists, so `query.get("msg", [""])[0]` gives the value. Finish with `return [text.encode("utf-8")]`.
lessons.explanation:
This is what every Python web framework does at its core: read `environ`, pick a handler, call `start_response`, return bytes. Frameworks add routing tables, request objects and templates on top.

Returning a list rather than a single `bytes` value matters. A `bytes` object is itself iterable, one integer at a time, and servers expect each item to be `bytes`.

lessons.title: Flask routes
lessons.body:
# Flask routes

Flask maps URLs to functions. A route returns a value, and Flask builds the response. Returning a dict or list sends JSON.

```python
from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.get("/users/<int:user_id>")
def user(user_id):
    return {"id": user_id}

@app.post("/users")
def add():
    data = request.get_json(silent=True)
    return {"ok": True}, 201
```

- A route may return `(body, status)`.
- `<int:x>` only matches digits and passes an `int`, so other text gets a 404.
- `abort(404)` stops with that status.
- `get_json(silent=True)` returns `None` rather than an error for a body that is not JSON.

## Testing without a server

`app.test_client()` drives the whole app through WSGI with no socket, which suits a phone well. In larger apps, a `create_app()` function builds a fresh app and fresh state for each test.
lessons.task: Finish `create_app()`. `POST /items` with JSON `{"name": "tea"}` stores an item with the next id from 1 and returns it with status 201. A body with no non-empty `name`, or a body that is not JSON, returns status 400 with `{"error": ...}`. `GET /items/<int:item_id>` returns the item or a 404.

checks.name: starts empty
checks.code:
client = create_app().test_client()
resp = client.get("/items")
assert resp.status_code == 200, resp.status_code
assert resp.get_json() == [], resp.get_json()

checks.name: creates items with rising ids
checks.code:
client = create_app().test_client()
first = client.post("/items", json={"name": "tea"})
second = client.post("/items", json={"name": "milk"})
assert first.status_code == 201, first.status_code
assert first.get_json() == {"id": 1, "name": "tea"}, first.get_json()
assert second.get_json() == {"id": 2, "name": "milk"}, second.get_json()
assert len(client.get("/items").get_json()) == 2, "both items should be listed"

checks.name: rejects bad bodies
checks.code:
client = create_app().test_client()
for kwargs in [{"json": {}}, {"json": {"name": ""}}, {"json": ["x"]}, {"data": "not json"}]:
    resp = client.post("/items", **kwargs)
    assert resp.status_code == 400, (kwargs, resp.status_code)
    assert "error" in resp.get_json(), resp.get_json()
assert client.get("/items").get_json() == [], "bad bodies should store nothing"

checks.name: fetches one item
checks.code:
client = create_app().test_client()
client.post("/items", json={"name": "tea"})
resp = client.get("/items/1")
assert resp.status_code == 200, resp.status_code
assert resp.get_json() == {"id": 1, "name": "tea"}, resp.get_json()

checks.name: missing items are 404
checks.code:
client = create_app().test_client()
assert client.get("/items/99").status_code == 404, "unknown id"
assert client.get("/items/abc").status_code == 404, "not a number"

checks.name: apps do not share state
checks.code:
one = create_app().test_client()
two = create_app().test_client()
one.post("/items", json={"name": "tea"})
assert two.get("/items").get_json() == [], "each app should start empty"

hints: Add two functions inside `create_app`, using `@app.post("/items")` and `@app.get("/items/<int:item_id>")`. `items` stays local to the app.
`request.get_json(silent=True)` may return `None` or a list, so confirm it is a dict before reading `name`.
`return {"error": "name is required"}, 400` for bad input. `item = {"id": len(items) + 1, "name": name}`, append it, then `return item, 201`. Import `abort` for the 404.
lessons.explanation:
`create_app` gives each test a clean app, so no test depends on what another left behind. Bigger projects use the same pattern with a database connection.

`Flask("todo")` passes an import name, which Flask uses to find templates and static files. In a real module, `Flask(__name__)` is the convention.

The list scan is `O(n)`. A dict keyed by id would be `O(1)`, and a real app would use a database.

lessons.title: How Django routes URLs
lessons.body:
# How Django routes URLs

Django is a full framework. A project holds apps, and each app usually has models (database tables as classes), views (functions from request to response), and templates (HTML). Requests pass through middleware, then the URL dispatcher picks a view.

Routes are listed in `urls.py`:

```python
urlpatterns = [
    path("articles/", index),
    path("articles/<int:year>/", by_year),
    path("u/<str:name>/", profile),
]
```

## The rules

- Routes have no leading slash.
- The list is tried in order, and the first match wins.
- A converter captures one part: `<int:x>` matches digits and gives an `int`, and `<str:x>` matches any text except `/`. A plain `<x>` means `str`.
- Captured values reach the view as keyword arguments.
- The whole path must match, so a missing trailing slash is a different URL.
- If nothing matches, the result is a 404.

The exercise builds this logic with no Django at all, so you can see that it is ordinary code.
lessons.task: Write `resolve(url, patterns)`, where `patterns` is a list of `(route, view)` tuples using `<int:x>`, `<str:x>` or `<x>`. Return `(view, kwargs)` for the first full match, with int captures converted. Raise the given `NotFound` when nothing matches.

checks.name: static routes
checks.code:
routes = [("about/", "about"), ("articles/", "index")]
assert resolve("articles/", routes) == ("index", {}), resolve("articles/", routes)

checks.name: converts ints and keeps strings
checks.code:
routes = [("articles/<int:year>/", "year"), ("u/<str:name>/", "user"), ("t/<tag>/", "tag")]
assert resolve("articles/2024/", routes) == ("year", {"year": 2024}), resolve("articles/2024/", routes)
assert resolve("u/ada/", routes) == ("user", {"name": "ada"}), resolve("u/ada/", routes)
assert resolve("t/42/", routes) == ("tag", {"tag": "42"}), resolve("t/42/", routes)

checks.name: several captures
checks.code:
routes = [("a/<int:y>/<int:m>/<str:slug>/", "post")]
got = resolve("a/2024/5/hi-there/", routes)
assert got == ("post", {"y": 2024, "m": 5, "slug": "hi-there"}), got

checks.name: first match wins
checks.code:
routes = [("a/<str:x>/", "first"), ("a/b/", "second")]
assert resolve("a/b/", routes)[0] == "first", resolve("a/b/", routes)

checks.name: strict matching

hints: Turn each route into a regular expression, and use `fullmatch` so that the whole URL has to match.
Use `re.finditer` to find each `<...>` capture. Escape the text between captures with `re.escape`, and use a named group for each capture: `(?P<name>[0-9]+)` or `(?P<name>[^/]+)`.
After `regex.fullmatch(url)`, `match.groupdict()` gives the kwargs as strings. Convert the `int` ones, return `(view, kwargs)`, and `raise NotFound(url)` after the loop.
lessons.explanation:
Django does essentially this: it compiles each route to a regular expression and walks the list in order. Matching is therefore `O(number of routes)`, which is why order can matter for both behaviour and speed.

`re.escape` keeps literal text literal, so the `.` in `d.e/` cannot match any character. Non-digit captures can never reach `int()`, because the regex has already rejected them.
